retrieved_chunks.text:
## ABSTRACT 

Binary systems are extremely common and influence many areas of astrophysics, such as stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. In this work, we introduce `flexAE` , a framework that combines a classical autoencoder architecture with a dedicated classifier component. It is designed to distinguish between single stars and binary systems based on their broadband spectral energy distributions, using all available photometry simultaneously while accounting for observational uncertainties. We demonstrate the capability of `flexAE` by using it to identify unresolved main sequence binaries in the outskirts of the 47 Tucanae globular cluster (NGC 104) with photometric data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We train the model on a simulated sample of single star and binary systems created with stellar atmosphere models. The model accurately reconstructs the photometric input features and achieves a classification accuracy of 0.85 on the simulated test set. We then apply the trained model to a sample of 1,424 cluster members found in Rubin DP1 with reliable _gri_ photometry, of which 32 are identified by the model as unresolved main sequence binaries. This corresponds to an observed binary fraction of 2 _._ 2[+0] _−_ 0 _[.] ._[5] 3[%.][We][estimate][that][the][intrinsic][main][sequence][binary][fraction][lies][between][3] _[.]_[7][+0] _−_ 0 _[.] ._[8] 5[%][and] 7 _._ 5[+1] _−_ 1 _[.] ._[5] 1[%.][The][binary][fraction][stays][constant][between][18] _[ −]_[36][arcmin][(5] _[.]_[7] _[ −]_[11] _[.]_[4][half-light][radii)][from] the cluster center. We highlight that `flexAE` can be easily adapted for other use cases. This makes `flexAE` well-suited for large-scale binary classification in upcoming wide-field surveys, such as Rubin LSST. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tobiasgeron/flexAE.

retrieved_chunks.text:
## 5. CONCLUSION 

In this work, we introduced `flexAE` , a novel and adaptable AE architecture designed to identify unresolved binary systems using multi-band photometry. This framework is, in simple terms, essentially a multidimensional CMD. However, we are able to use information from all available bands simultaneously and explicitly account for observational uncertainties. Furthermore, the AE finds the most efficient way to classify single stars and binary systems in this high-dimensional parameter space, as opposed to following an isochrone. 

It also organizes its latent space in such a way that is optimal for classification by training a classifier component at the same time as the encoder and decoder components. Another main advantage of this approach is that, in principle, we could be sensitive to binary systems with lower mass-ratios (and thus lower flux ratios), though it depends on the quality of the photometry and wavelength coverage. Finally, it is trivial to add additional bands to the analysis as they become available. 

We use `flexAE` to find MS+MS binaries in the outskirts of 47 Tucanae. We trained and validated the framework with a simulated dataset of single star and binary systems created with the stellar atmosphere templates from F. Castelli & R. L. Kurucz (2003) convolved with the throughput curves of Rubin DP1. The model was able to robustly reconstruct the input features, achieved a classification accuracy of 0.85 on the simulated test set, and demonstrated a strongly bimodal prediction probability (ˆ _y_ ). We also showed that we can use the latent space of the model to identify anomalies and out-of-distribution targets by using the mean distance to the 10 nearest neighbors in the latent space ( _d_[¯] 10) alongside the reconstruction loss ( _L_ rec).

results.reference_answer: They (1) identified bound systems (bound companions) around massive stars from their N-body gradual cluster-formation simulations, and (2) constructed projected stellar density profiles around massive stars; both metrics were computed at a fiducial age of 3 Myr for model–observation comparisons (sections 2.1–2.3 and the choice of 3 Myr in section 3).
results.answer:
At the fiducial cluster age t = 3.0 Myr the authors computed the average number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ around massive stars (and examined its dependence on cloud surface density Σcloud, Mcl model, companion mass threshold, and star location subsets: central, offset, ejected). [1] [2]

Using the fiducial (ε_ff = 0.03) simulations the authors computed and compared the distributions of projected companion separations and companion-to-primary mass ratios (for bound companions around massive stars ≥ 16.0 M⊙) against observations from the SMASH+ survey. [3] [4]

gathered or lost during dynamical interactions with other stars in the forming star cluster (Heggie 1975; Hills 1975; Wall et al. 2019). 

The relative contribution of these mechanisms to the observed multiplicity remains an area of active research (Offner et al. 2023). These mechanisms should leave imprints on the separation and massratio distribution of companions, however the completeness and bias of these observations should be carefully considered. Moreover, these primordial signatures could be masked by subsequent dynamical processing. So, it is important to study the multiplicity of massive stars in young star clusters before significant dynamical interactions have occurred (Offner et al. 2023). To complement this, one could use _𝑁_ -body simulations to quantify the level of dynamical processing that occurs on a population of primordial companions around massive stars. 

Different theories of massive star formation have different predictions about the primordial multiplicity of massive stars. For example, Turbulent Core Accretion (McKee & Tan 2003), especially in magnetically supported cores, can produce initially relatively isolated massive cores and thus stars. A certain level of clustering of companions around these massive stars could then develop subsequently via dynamical evolution in the environment of a forming star cluster. On the other hand, Competitive Accretion (Bonnell et al. 2001; Wang et al. 2010; Grudić et al. 2022) predicts the ubiquitous presence of many low-mass companions around a massive star, even from its earliest stages of formation. This presents a way to distinguish between these two massive star formation models by studying the clustering of lower-mass companions around massive stars in young star-forming regions. 

We expect that this may be accomplished by the consideration of surface density profiles of young stellar objects (YSOs) around massive protostars (i.e., while still accreting) and recently formed massive stars. Such surface number density profiles around massive stars have been studied using both observations (Costa Silva et al. 2022; Crowe et al. 2024), and simulations of star cluster formation (Grudić et al. 2022). Such comparisons with observed systems help us to understand whether massive stars can form in relative isolation or need to have companions present, shedding light on their dominant formation mechanism.

## **4.3 Companion properties** 

We have 50% primordial binaries, but no primordial triples and/or multiple systems. However, we found that massive stars gathered many lower-mass companions via dynamical interactions after they are formed in the simulation. We compared the projected separations and mass ratios of companions around massive stars above 16 _𝑀_ ⊙ in our simulations with observed companions around O-stars in the `SMASH+` survey. We found a similar drop-off in equal-mass companions beyond a certain distance. They noted a decline after 100 au, whereas we found a decline after 1000 au. The fact that we find massive companions further out is probably because our massive stars are part of a forming star cluster with higher stellar densities around them, whereas `SMASH+` survey includes field stars. So, some dynamical processing may have stripped the companions beyond 100 au around these stars after star cluster formation and expansion was complete. 

In addition, we find close binary companions to massive stars within 10 au of our massive stars, some of which have formed dynamically. Chon & Vigna-Gómez (2026) used their star cluster simulations to note that such close binary systems can form through the hardening of the binary due to circumbinary disc-driven migration. On the other hand, we lack close triple companions in our simulations. We infer that these close triple companions around observed O-stars must have been formed primordially. These primordial companions could be formed via fragmentation in a core or disk, with the remnant gas possibly driving migration to tighten the orbits of the bound triple system.

## **3.1 Effect of location and stellar mass** 

We classified massive stars into three subsets: _central stars_ , _offset stars_ and _ejected stars_ to study the effect of cluster environment on their bound companions. Table 2 presents statistics of primary massive stars across these subsets in our simulations across all ( _𝑀_ cl, Σcloud, _𝜖_ ff) models at _𝑡_ = 3 Myr. Figures below show the results for our fiducial _𝜖_ ff = 0.03 model, unless otherwise specified. These primary massive stars have their own independent systems of bound companions (if any). We find that _ejected_ subset comprised a range of 1-30% of the primary massive star population at _𝑡_ = 3.0 Myr, depending on the model. The dynamical state of the forming star cluster determined the relative fraction of _central_ and _offset_ stars in the remaining stars that are still bound to the cluster. 

In Figure 1, we show the mass _𝑀★_ of the massive stars versus the number of bound companions ( _𝑁_ comp) around them. We find that more massive stars tend to have more companions than lower-mass stars, as expected. However, _𝑁_ bound depends on the environment of the massive star as well. For similar _𝑀★_ , two massive stars can have different _𝑁_ bound in the same star cluster depending on their location. We find that a _central star_ tends to have more companions than an _ejected star_ of the same mass. For instance, we find that _ejected stars_ tend to be mostly singles ( _𝑁_ bound = 0) or binaries ( _𝑁_ bound = 1) across all our models. Only a few of them have more than one companion, with those companions having small mass-ratios compared to the massive star.

## _3.4.2 Comparison of companion properties_ 

Figure 12 shows the separation and mass-ratio of bound companions around all massive stars with masses ≥ 16 _._ 0 _𝑀_ ⊙ in our simulations. We compare them with observed companions around O-stars from the Southern Massive Stars at High Angular Resolution survey ( `SMASH+;` Tramper et al. 2025). This high angular resolution interferometric survey targeted nearby O-stars in the Southern hemisphere ( _𝛿<_ 0[◦] ) and identified companions around them. In addition to the comparison of full set of companions, we compare the different orders of companions separately, focusing on the binary and tertiary companions. We found M300L and M300H models to be the most comparable to their observations, because massive stars in higher _𝑀_ cl models have fewer companions (mostly singles or binaries, hence the smaller ⟨ _𝑁_ bound⟩). 

The survey had reported a relative scarcity of massive companions at large separations beyond 100 au, with few companions above _𝑞_ > 0.8 at such distances, which were mostly upper limits (Tramper et al. 2025). We observe a similar trend in our simulated companions in the M300 models, with large-distance companions having small mass ratios ( _𝑞<_ 0 _._ 4) beyond 1000 au. On the other hand, the `SMASH+` survey found close binary and tertiary companions within 10 au of some of these O-stars. In our simulations, we reproduce close binaries however, we lack close triple companions. Our closest triple companions are at separations of 100s of au. We discuss the implications of this lack of close triple companions in section 4.3. 

For M300L and M300H models, we ran two-sample KolmogorovSmirnov (K-S) test to check whether the similarity of the simulated and observed companion distributions for both separations and massratios. The results of the K-S test are presented in Table 4. We found that both M300L and M300H models were similar to the observed triple separations while only M300L was similar to the observed binary separations. For mass-ratios however, we did not find similarity between simulated and observed companions in these models.

## ABSTRACT 

We address the origin of the Little Red Dots (LRDs) seen by JWST at cosmic morning ( _𝑧_ = 4−8) as compact stellar systems with over-massive black holes (BHs). We propose that LRDs form naturally after feedbackfree starbursts (FFB) in thousands of star clusters and following wet compaction. Analytically, we show how the clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and BHs to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk. The clusters merge to form compact central stellar systems as observed. Mutual tidal stripping does not qualitatively affect the analysis. The young, rotating clusters are natural sites for the formation of BH seeds via rapid core collapse. The migrating clusters carry the BH seeds, which merge into central super-massive BHs (SMBHs). Compactions are required to deepen the potential wells such that the SMBHs are retained after post-merger gravitational-wave recoils, locked to the galaxy centers. Using cosmological simulations at different epochs, with different codes and physical recipes, we evaluate the additional growth of LRD-matching compact central stellar systems by global compaction events. Adding to the dry growth by cluster mergers, the compactions can increase the escape velocities to retain the SMBHs. The LRDs appear at _𝑧_ ∼ 8, after the formation of FFB clusters, and disappear after _𝑧_ ∼ 4 when the stellar mass is above 10[9] _𝑀_ ⊙ by growing post-compaction blue disks around the nuclear LRDs. The LRD abundance is expected to be ∼ 10[−][5] −10[−][4] Mpc[−][3] , increasing from _𝑧_ ∼ 4 to _𝑧_ ∼ 8.

## 1.1. _Little Red Dots_ 

JWST observations reveal the existence of a distinct population of galaxies termed Little Red Dots (LRDs), detected at cosmic morning in the redshift range _𝑧_ = 4 − 8 (e.g., G. Barro et al. 2024a,b; J. F. W. Baggen et al. 2024; F. Pacucci 2024; F. Pacucci & R. Narayan 2024; C. M. Casey et al. 2024, 2025; J. E. Greene et al. 2025; H. B. Akins et al. 2025a,b,c; F. Pacucci & A. Loeb 2025; F. Pacucci et al. 2025; A. J. Taylor et al. 2025b,a). Their high abundance is roughly 1 _._ 5−2 dex below the total abundance of galaxies at the same UV magnitude (e.g., V. Kokorev et al. 2024; J. E. Greene et al. 2024; D. D. Kocevski et al. 2025). The LRDs are characterized by compact, mostly unresolved red optical sizes. They tend to show a so called “V-shaped” spectral energy distribution (SED), blue in the UV and red in optical light. They show 

broad permitted lines, with a flat IR spectrum, no far-IR/submm emission and weak near-to-mid IR emission, and some show Balmer breaks. Typically, no X-ray or radio waves are detected. 

The two extreme interpretations of LRDs are that they are either dominated by black holes (BHs) or by stars (e.g., F. Pacucci 2024; F. Pacucci & R. Narayan 2024). The BHdominated interpretation would require a very high ratio of BH-to-stellar mass compared to low redshifts and an explanation for the undetected X-rays. The stellar-dominated interpretation would require extremely high stellar densities, not seen in other galaxies.

## 1.2. _FFB clusters_ 

A straightforward physical model predicts a high starformation efficiency, at the level of 0 _._ 2 − 0 _._ 3 for the global ratio of stars to accreted gas, under the conditions of high density and moderate metallicity that are valid in massive galaxies at cosmic dawn (A. Dekel et al. 2023; Z. Li et al. 2024). It is due to feedback-free starbursts (FFB) in thousands of star clusters within each galaxy. This is as opposed to the a star formation efficiency lower than 0 _._ 1 at lower redshifts, where feedback from stars and from AGN is expected to suppress star formation. The FFB phase is expected to occur at _𝑧>_ 8, in dark-matter halos of mass _𝑀_ vir _>_ 10[10] _[.]_[5] _𝑀_ ⊙, with the threshold mass dropping steeply as a function of redshift, _𝑀_ vir ∝(1 + _𝑧_ )[−][6] _[.]_[2] . The typical resultant galaxy is a rather compact rotating disk of half-mass radius ∼ 300 pc, consisting of thousands of rotating star clusters of masses in the range 10[4] −10[7] _𝑀_ ⊙ and radii of order 10 pc. These galaxies are predicted to have low gas fraction ( _𝑓_ gas ∼ 0 _._ 01−0 _._ 1), relatively low metallicity ( _𝑍_ ∼ 0 _._ 01 − 0 _._ 1 _𝑍_ ⊙), and low dust attenuation ( _𝐴_ UV ∼ 0 _._ 5). We propose that the FFB clusters serve as a key element in the formation of LRDs, both in the origin of a compact stellar system and in the growth of an over-massive central black hole.

retrieved_chunks.text:
The major compaction events, those that trigger a decisive long-term quenching process and a transition from central dark-matter to baryon dominance, tend to occur near the golden mass, halos of masses 10[11] −10[12] _𝑀_ ⊙ (A. Dekel et al. 2019) at all redshifts. Thisis seenin cosmological simulations (M. Tomassetti et al. 2016) and in machine-learning-aided comparisons to observations (M. Huertas-Company et al. 2018). This preferred mass scale for major compaction events seems to be due, at least partly, to the physical processes of supernova feedback and hot circum-galactic medium (CGM), which tend to suppress compaction attempts at lower and higher masses, respectively. At cosmic dawn, the FFB halos are indeed of masses ∼ 10[11] _𝑀_ ⊙, in the vicinity of the golden mass, and they correspond to high-sigma peaks of _>_ 4 _𝜎_ (A. Dekel et al. 2025a), which tend to have more frequent and stronger compaction events due to multiple colliding streams with low angular momentum (Y. Dubois et al. 2012). 

The compaction events trigger a sequence of morphological changes, which may be relevant both to the beginning and the end of the LRD phase. The compaction events drive central starbursts in the form of blue nuggets, followed by insideout quenching to quiescent red nuggets, as a result of gas depletion due to star formation and the associated outflows (S. Tacchella et al. 2016b,a). 

We use here cosmological simulations, utilizing a variety of codes and physical models at different epochs, to quantify the compaction-driven growth of compact, massive central stellar systems, beyond their growth by dry mergers between the clusters. These compact central stellar systems could plausibly be identified with the stellar systems of LRDs, and could possibly increase the escape velocities to the level that is required for retaining the SMBHs at the centers against GW recoils.

Figure 5 shows face-on images of gas and stellar densities during the stages of a typical compaction event (in galaxy V07) at _𝑧_ ∼ 3 _._ 2. It demonstrates the merger-driven gas contraction to a star-bursting “blue nugget”, the following passive stellar evolution to a compact “red nugget”, and the subsequent formation of an extended star-forming gas disk and ring. This disk/ring, which is fed by incoming cold streams, is stabilized by the compaction-driven formation of a central mass (A. Dekel et al. 2020b). The red nugget may resemble an LRD, while the appearance of an extended blue disk marks the end of the phase that is observationally identified as an LRD. 

Figure 6 shows zoom-in images of post-compaction densities of another VELA galaxy (V12), at _𝑧_ = 4, demonstrating the formation of a star-forming nuclear disk. The mean surface density within 100 pc is ∼ 5×10[5] _𝑀_ ⊙ pc[−][2] . This implies a mass of 3×10[9] _𝑀_ ⊙, and an escape velocity of ∼ 520 km s[−][1] . 

At higher redshifts, for a given mass, the radius should scale as (1 + _𝑧_ )[−][1] , and the 3D and 2D densities should scale as (1 + _𝑧_ )[3] and (1 + _𝑧_ )[2] . As discussed below in §8, this naturally predicts a redshift dependence of the stellar-system compactness, and therefore of the abundance of LRDs as selected by their compactness, a dependence that is consistent with the observed trend (B. L. Jones et al. 2025).

## _3.1.2 Gas clumps_ 

The left panel of Fig. 4 shows the one-dimensional probability distribution functions (PDFs) of the masses, _𝑀_ c, of identified gas clumps. Because of the particle-number threshold adopted in the GMC identification algorithm, gas clumps with _𝑀_ c ≲ 5 × 10[4] M⊙ cannot be identified. We find that the mass distributions strongly depend on the compactness of the host galaxies. In all simulations, the PDFs peak 

at _𝑀_ c ≈ 10[4] _[.]_[8] M⊙ which is close to the minimum mass of identified GMCs, whereas the maximum clump mass increases significantly towards higher _𝑧_ . The maximum masses reach ∼ 10[5] _[.]_[1] , 10[6] _[.]_[3] , and 10[7] _[.]_[4] M⊙ for the _𝑧_ = 0, 6, and 10 cases, respectively. Although massive clumps become progressively rarer at higher masses, the overall mass distributions broaden substantially in more compact galaxies. These results indicate that compact high- _𝑧_ galaxies preferentially form more massive GMCs over a wider mass range.

Applying this model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[[11]] M⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift _𝑧_ = 0–10, we find that more compact discs form more massive and denser clumps. The maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] to ∼ 10[7] M⊙, and the fraction of clumps exceeding the surface density of 300 M⊙⊙ pc[[−][2]][[2]] rises from 0 _._ 25 to 0 _._ 38 between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes. Star formation becomes correspondingly bursty, and the global star formation efficiency after three disc rotations increases from 5 × 10[−][3] to 2 × 10[−][1] in 10[[10]] M⊙⊙ haloes and from 2 × 10 × 10 10[[−][2]][[2]] to 4 × 10 × 10 10[[−][1]][[1]] in 10[[11]] M⊙⊙ haloes as the redshift increases from _𝑧_ = 0 to 10. The accompanying feedback disrupts the gas discs of the most compact systems, while prominent stellar spiral arms emerge. Self-gravitationally bound star clusters form only in compact discs. We find no bound star clusters at _𝑧_ ≤ 2 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes, whereas the bound cluster mass fraction reaches ≈ ≈ 40 per cent at _𝑧_ ≥ 8 and ≈ ≈ 70 per cent in the most compact 10[11] M⊙ halo.

## **5 CONCLUSION** 

We have investigated how the compactness of galactic discs regulates clumpy star formation and the formation of bound star clusters. To this end, we have developed a new star formation model (CSF) in which star-forming gas clumps are identified on-the-fly and converted into stars with an efficiency _𝜖_ SF set by the clump surface density Σc, calibrated against the radiation hydrodynamics simulations of Fukushima & Yajima (2021). We apply the model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[11] M⊙ with a fixed gas-to-halo mass ratio of 0 _._ 01, adopting disc scale radii 

appropriate for _𝑧_ = 0–10 as a proxy for compactness. Our main results are summarised as follows. 

(i) Compact discs form more massive and denser gas clumps. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] _[.]_[1] to 10[7] _[.]_[4] M⊙ and the maximum clump surface density from ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[9] to _>_ 10[4] _[.]_[0] M⊙ pc[−][2] between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10. The fraction of clumps exceeding Σc _,_ th = 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] rises from 0 _._ 25 at _𝑧_ = 0 to 0 _._ 34 at _𝑧_ = 6 and 0 _._ 38 at _𝑧_ = 10, and the most compact discs host clumps with _𝜖_ SF ∼ 1.

(iv) Self-gravitationally bound star clusters form only in compact discs. results.question: Compare the structural implications for low-density volume-filling gas in (1) the H II regions study "H II region filling factors in NGC 628: Luminosity-size relation and connection with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission" and (2) the study "Dust destruction in bubbles driven by multiple supernovae explosions". Specifically: (a) What does each paper report about the presence and persistence of low-density gas occupying large volumes (i.e., low filling factor or hot tenuous gas) in their respective systems? (b) Based on the cited results, how do the papers differ in the factors that control the amount and observational signatures of that low-density gas? Please cite supporting excerpts from both papers.
results.reference_answer:
(a) Presence and persistence of low-density volume-filling gas:
- H II regions in NGC 628: Luminous giant and supergiant H II regions show a decrease in the ionized-gas filling factor (FF) with increasing volume, meaning larger regions are characterized by more widely spaced clumps and a larger fraction of low-density gas occupying the available volume. However, volume alone explains little of the FF scatter (R^2_fit ≃ 0.16–0.21) [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0].
- Multi-SN bubbles: In bubbles evolved in a clumpy medium, dust (and associated material) can be dispersed into the hot interior and remain there on longer timescales (several Myr) when SN explosions are frequent (more frequent than one per ~30 kyr). The hot interior can thus contain dispersed material and remain a bright IR source for Myr timescales; the hot plasma is maintained at ~2–4×10^6 K for SN rates of one per ~100–5 kyr [evidence_id: 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].

(b) Factors controlling amount and observational signatures of low-density gas and differences between papers:
- H II regions (NGC 628): The key control is structural clump spacing within the ionized region: larger physical volume implies more widely spaced clumps and a larger fraction of low-density gas. However, the paper emphasizes that volume alone is insufficient to explain the observed FF scatter, implying additional physical factors (e.g., internal structure, density variations, catalog/method choices) influence FF [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0; also discussion of methodological effects on measured relations in D.1 indicates which observables are radius-independent and which are not, affecting interpretation].
- Multi-SN bubbles: The dominant controls are the ambient medium structure (clumpiness / density contrast) and the SN cadence. In a clumpy medium, stripped dense lumps and swept-up dust replenish the hot interior, prolonging IR emission; high SN frequency prevents dust exhaustion and sustains hot tenuous gas and IR/X-ray signatures. The IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratio for multi-SN bubbles typically ranges ~1–30 and depends weakly on SN rate but strongly on ambient density contrast (higher destruction of clouds in more homogeneous media reduces IR emission) [evidence_id: 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].

Summary synthesis: Both studies identify low-density, volume-filling components in their systems (ionized low-density gas in large H II regions; hot tenuous gas in multi-SN bubbles). The H II-region result attributes larger low-density fraction primarily to geometrical/structural scaling (larger regions with more widely spaced clumps) but finds volume alone is a poor predictor, whereas the multi-SN bubble study attributes persistence and observational visibility of low-density hot gas mainly to dynamical factors (SN frequency) and the ambient medium clumpiness, which determine dust survival and IR vs X-ray emission balance [evidence_id: 03f11027f87d37771b2883f0; 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4].
results.answer:
Aragüete Riesco et al. (H II regions in NGC 628) report that low filling-factor H II regions occupy regimes with log(FF) ≈ -5.01 to -4.02 and that lower FF is associated with more extended, diffuse ionized structures. [1] [2]

Aragüete Riesco et al. report that regions with lower log(FF) values exhibit higher PAH-to-dust ratio R_PAH, indicating less efficient PAH processing (i.e., more PAH survival) in more porous/low-FF structures. [2] [3]

Vasiliev & Nath report that in bubbles evolving in a clumpy medium dust can be dispersed into the hot gas on longer timescales (exceeding several Myr) for SN explosions more frequent than one SN per 30 kyr, allowing the bubble to remain a bright IR source up to several Myr. [4]

Vasiliev & Nath state that the forward shock of the bubble moves in the interclump low-density medium and maintains high velocity there, while parts of the shock that interact with dense clumps penetrate them with lower velocity and form hot envelopes around the clumps, which supply dust into the hot gas. [5]

Vasiliev & Nath report that continuous SNe produce multiple shocks and high-velocity sound waves that strip surviving dense clumps and replenish dust into the hot gas, increasing the duration that dust and hot tenuous gas coexist in the bubble interior. [5] [6]

Vasiliev & Nath report that for bubbles driven by multiple SNe the IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratio typically ranges between ≈1–30, weakly dependent on SN rate but sensitive to the ambient medium density contrast (σ); decreasing density contrast reduces IR emission and thus the observable dust signature. [4]

Comparison — presence and persistence: the H II regions paper emphasizes low volumetric filling factors (log(FF) down to ≈ -5) associated with diffuse ionized gas that favors PAH survival, whereas the multiple-SNe bubble paper emphasizes a persistent hot, low-density plasma (T_X ∼ 2–4×10^6 K) inside bubbles that can be long-lived (dust dispersed into hot gas for > several Myr) when SN cadence is high and the medium is clumpy. [2] [3] [4]

Comparison — controlling factors and observational signatures: the H II region study attributes the amount and observational signature of low-density/volume-filling ionized gas primarily to ionizing photon rate, volumetric Hα luminosity density, and filling factor (which control PAH photodissociation and R_PAH), while the SNe bubble study attributes the amount and observables of hot tenuous gas to SN rate (cadence), ambient medium clumpiness/density contrast (σ), and shock–clump interactions (which control dust replenishment, IR vs X-ray emission and dust survival). [1] [3] [4] [6]

Method/observable differences relevant to low-density gas: Aragüete Riesco et al. use Hα-based volumetric luminosity density, ionizing photon rate, filling factor and JWST/MIRI PAH-to-dust ratio R_PAH as diagnostics of porosity and PAH survival, whereas Vasiliev & Nath use 3-D hydrodynamical simulations of clustered SNe, tracking gas temperature, shock propagation, clump stripping and dust sputtering to predict X-ray and IR emission and dust survival timescales. [3] [4] [7] [8]

We examined the relation between FF and PAH emission. The transition in PAH abundance identified in the log(RPAH)log(LHα/R) relation corresponds to H II regions with volumetric Hα luminosity density, log(LHα/R[3] ) ≈ 31.76-32.11 erg s[−][1] pc[−][3] , ionizing photon rates log(QH) ≈ 49.03 - 49.48 s[−][1] ), and log(FF) ≈ -5.01- -4.02. The consistency of these three independent diagnostics in two catalogs, built from different instruments and radius definition methods, confirms that this physical regime marks the onset of efficient PAH photodissociation in H II regions of NGC 628, in agreement with the critical threshold log(QH) ≳ 10[50] s[−][1] reported by Egorov et al. (2023b). 

Within the luminous giant and supergiant H II region regime, characterized by high FF values, we find a clear dependence between the PAH-to-dust fraction and FF. PAHs are highly susceptible to Lyman-continuum radiation, undergoing photoionization and photodissociation that progressively reduce their PAH fraction (Dale et al. 2025). High-FF regions, which are typically the most luminous, provide the intense radiation fields required for efficient PAH destruction. In addition, stellar winds and radiation pressure from massive O/B stars can evacuate the central regions and compress dust and gas into shell-like structures where PAH emission is preferentially detected (Watson et al. 2008). Our results suggest that lower-luminosity H II regions exhibit higher PAH-to-dust ratios, indicating less efficient destruction of PAHs and carbonaceous grains, consistent with the findings of Egorov et al. (2023b, 2025). Beyond reduced photodestruction, evolutionary effects may also contribute: the shattering of larger carbonaceous grains and the preferential destruction of VSGs can enhance the relative PAH abundance in older H II regions (Jones et al. 1996; Galliano et al. 2008; Micelotta et al. 2010; Seok et al. 2014). Our observations support this scenario

retrieved_chunks.text:
## **ABSTRACT** 

_Aims._ Understanding the internal structure of H II regions is fundamental for constraining star formation processes in galaxies. We investigated how the filling factor (FF) relates to luminosity, size, electron density, and Hα equivalent width (EW(Hα)) in H II regions. We also explored the association between star-forming regions and the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-to-dust emission, to assess their possible connection to the evolutionary stages of H II regions. 

_Methods._ We investigated the FF in 622 H II regions in NGC 628 by combining 475 regions from SIGNALS and 147 from PHANGSMUSE using a dedicated analysis pipeline. We derived the luminosity, emission line fluxes, radii, electron densities, and FF. We used PHANGS-JWST survey images to study the spatial relation between the FF and PAH-to-dust emission, quantified by the PAH-to-dust ratio _RPAH_ using James Webb Space Telescope/Mid-Infrared Instrument (JWST/MIRI) emission bands at 7.7, 11.3, and 21 µm. _Results._ Higher Log(FF) and high EW(Hα) values are found in luminous regions, whereas more extended regions with lower EW(Hα) display lower Log(FF) values. We show that the H II radius definition significantly affects the LHα − R relation. Low-luminosity compact H II regions appear to reflect a transition from cluster-powered regions to nebulae that are ionized by single massive stars, with the transition occurring around log(LHα) ∼ 37 erg s[−][1] . The PAH-to-dust ratio RPAH correlates with the volumetric Hα luminosity density, LHα/R[3] , with a transitional range centered around log(LHα/R[3] ) ∼ 32 erg s[−][1] , corresponding to log(FF) ≈−4.4. Regions with lower Log(FF) values exhibit higher RPAH values, suggesting less efficient PAH processing in more porous structures.

Furthermore, examination of emission line profiles provides insight into the kinematics of the gas, including expansion and turbulence along the line of sight. 

These H II regions produce characteristic optical emission, such as Hα, which is commonly used as a tracer of recent star formation on timescales shorter than 10 Myr (Kennicutt & Evans 2012). Observations reveal that H II regions exhibit complex internal structures, with dense zones embedded within lower-density gas and spanning a wide range of densities and temperatures (e.g., Castaneda et al. 1992). Several models have been proposed to describe these inhomogeneities. The first studies to characterize internal density fluctuations were conducted by Osterbrock & Flather (1959). They proposed that as a first approximation, H II regions can be modeled as spheres filled with low-density gas containing small optically thin highdensity clumps or condensations. These clumps form parsecscale substructures that are coherent in position-velocity space (Williams et al. 1999), and electron density variations within individual regions can be traced using density-sensitive emissionline ratios such as [S II].

SN remnants are bright IR sources until dust remains dispersed in hot gas inside the remnant. Dust grains located in hot gas can be destroyed by sputtering or move to gas in other thermal phases due to gas cooling or dynamical effects. Similar mechanisms occur in bubbles driven by multiple SNe explosions. 

In the previous sections we explored the questions as to how interstellar grains are destroyed in SNe-driven bubbles and how destruction of the swept-up dust exhausts after the shell cools down. This dust passes rapidly across the hot layer and accumulates mostly in the cold shell, with a negligible amount left in the hot inner region. Thus, the swept-up dust does not contribute in the IR emission of the bubble after the dust stops to be destroyed in the bubble shell or at _𝑡_ ∼ _[>] 𝑡𝑠𝑎𝑡_ (eq. 1), when the shell velocity is of the order of _𝑣_ 0 ∼100 km s[−1] . 

Meanwhile, dust is injected in hot interior of the bubble by every subsequent SN explosion. The injected grains can become a significant source of IR emission as long as they survive in this hostile environment. The grain lifetime is roughly _𝜏_ ∼10[5] _𝑎𝜇_ m _𝑛_[−1] H[yr,][and][if][this][timescale][is][shorter] than the time between subsequent SN explosions Δ _𝑡𝑆𝑁_ , then dust cannot accumulate in the hot interior. However, dust particles can leave the hot gas due to their high velocity, grains are caught up with the bubble shell and move in to colder gas, where they cannot emit efficiently.

retrieved_chunks.text: In the bubbles evolving in a clumpy medium, the dust mass in hot gas is replenished by not only swept-up unprocessed interstellar dust, but also from stripped dense gaseous lumps far behind the forward shock of the bubble. Owing to the latter process, dust can be dispersed in the hot gas on longer timescales, exceeding several Myr, for SNe explosions more frequent than one SN per 30 kyr (see Fig. 9). Therefore, a bubble evolving in a clumpy medium can remain a bright IR source up to several Myr. Simultaneously, the hot plasma inside the bubble emits in X-ray. Due to continuous SNe explosions the plasma temperature is supported at _𝑇𝑋_ ∼(2 −4) × 10[6] K for SNe rate of one SN per ∼100 −5 kyr in bubbles older than several tens of kyr. Using the approach described in the paper (Dedikov and Vasiliev, 2025a), we calculate the ratio between the IR and X-ray luminosities averaged over the whole bubble driven by multi-SNe. Usually the IR-to-X-ray ratio is used to determine the contribution of dust cooling into radiative losses in hot plasma (Dwek, 1987). We find that the ratio typically ranges between ∼1–30. These values weakly depend on the SNe rate. However, a decrease of density contrast (density dispersion _𝜎_ ) in the ambient medium results in more efficient cloud destruction and, therefore, diminishing IR emission down to almost negligible values, for bubble older 100 kyr evolved in a homogeneous medium with _𝑛_ ∼1 cm[−3] .

Those parts of the shock that interact with the clumps and penetrate them with lower velocity and in which the dust locked in the denser clumps, remain protected against sputtering. Continuous SNe explosions result in multiple shocks so that high-velocity sound waves impinge on dense clumps that have survived the impact of the forward shock. These waves strip the clumps and form hot envelopes around them. Thus, deep behind the forward shock dust continues to income from destroyed gaseous fragments. As seen in Fig. 7, the first two processes (a) and (b) operate during about 300 kyr. The third one comes into play when all the remaining dust becomes locked in dense gas. 

During the first several hundreds of kyrs the fraction of surviving dust _𝑓𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑣_ remains higher in the bubble expanding in a clumpy medium than in the one expanding in a homogeneous one (Fig. 7). Later on, _𝑓𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑣_ in clumpy environment decreases because of continuous stripping of dense fragments (as seen in Fig. 7). Eventually at times _𝑡>_ 100 kyr the rate of surviving dust in a homogeneous medium becomes higher, because of the process (c) (of dust getting locked in dense clumps and destruction occurring only in the envelopes around them) becoming dominant at this phase, and at _𝑡_ ∼300 _[>]_ kyr the surviving fraction of dust in both cases turns to become of the same order. 

Fig. 8 presents the mass of dust destroyed in the bubble for the same SN rates as shown in Fig. 2, but evolving in a clumpy medium. At early times, this mass (of destroyed dust) in the bubble evolving in a clumpy medium is lower than that in a homogeneous one. For SN rate (Δ _𝑡_ )[−1] ∼ (100 kyr)[−1] the mass of dust destroyed during expansion in a clumpy medium begins to exceed the value reached in a homogeneous medium at an age of the bubble ∼300 kyr. For higher SN rate this crossing occurs earlier, at ≈150 kyr, for all other rates.

Dust destruction in bubbles driven by multiple-SNe 

by several features (e.g., mass, size, sort, id number etc) to allow one to identify their evolution and physical properties. To follow the transport of dust mass (not of an individual grain) in a gaseous flow we introduce a macroscopic mass of a ‘superparticle’ or macroparticle, which represents a conglomerate of microscopic grains. Thus, the dust component is modelled as an ensemble of macroparticles governed by the motion equations (see description in Appendix A of Vasiliev and Shchekinov, 2024). The backward reaction of dust on to gas due to momentum transfer, work done by the drag force and the frictional heating from dust particles are also accounted for in order to ensure both dynamical and thermal self-consistency. We take into account the destruction of dust particles by both thermal (in a hot gas) and kinetic (due to a relative motion between gas and grains) sputtering (Draine and Salpeter, 1979a). 

The mass of dust in a medium is distributed between many dust ‘superparticles’. Each ‘superparticle’ is supposed to represent an ensemble of numerous physical grains of a single size. To follow the dust transport in a medium we set at least one ‘superparticle’ per computational cell. Each ‘superparticle’ contains the total mass of the ensemble of single-sized dust particles in it. So the total dust mass in a cell is a sum of masses of ‘superparticles’ inside a cell (see for more details Vasiliev and Shchekinov, 2024). 

The cell size equal to 1 pc is adopted for the runs with ambient gas number density _𝑛_ = 1 cm[−3] . This is sufficient both for resolving the thermal (cooling) length estimated as _𝜆𝑡_ ∼5 _𝑛_[−1] _𝑇_ 6 pc and for reproducing the global bubble dynamics driven by multiple SNe (e.g., Fielding et al., 2018). The numerical grid consists of 256[3] cells. This results in the total number of interstellar dust ‘superparticles’ in the domain being 256[3] ∼16 millions.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Although clumps around SN remnants experience shock impact only once, the clumps in bubbles driven by multiple SNe suffer impacts from shocks episodically as long as the SNe explode. Each such encounter perturbs the medium enveloping the clump and strip it through the action of various hydrodynamic instabilities (Kelvin-Helmholtz, Rayleigh-Taylor and Richtmyer-Meshkov). This results in continuously repeated shock encounters, affecting the dust confined in clumps, and it increases the mass fraction of the destroyed dust. Despite this fact, the inner parts of clumps can survive continuous shock impacts due to radiative losses and strong density contrast. In such conditions, a substantial fraction of confined dust is protected against sputtering. 

To study the dust destruction in multiple-SNe driven bubbles, we construct a clumpy gas density field by making use of the module pyFC[1] (Lewis and Austin, 2002) which generates lognormal ‘fractal cubes’. Within this model the gas density fluctuations in the ambient medium have a lognormal distribution and a Kolmogorov power-law spectrum with spatial index _𝛽_ = 5∕3 and maximum size of inhomogeneities equal to 16 pc. The density field is characterised by the mean ⟨ _𝜌_ ⟩ and the standard deviation _𝜎_ for logarithmic value. We consider a density field with _𝜎_ = 2 _._ 2, which corresponds to the contrast for 2 _𝜎_ fluctuations exceeding a factor of ∼80 _>_ related to the mean value ⟨ _𝜌_ ⟩ = 1 cm−3. We assume pressure equilibrium at the initial state, i.e., _𝜌𝑇_ = const, with zero gas and dust velocities. Thus, the gas temperature values differ by a factor of ∼80 _[>]_ between dense cloudlets and the intercloud medium.

claims.text: Aragüete Riesco et al. (H II regions in NGC 628) report that low filling-factor H II regions occupy regimes with log(FF) ≈ -5.01 to -4.02 and that lower FF is associated with more extended, diffuse ionized structures.

Aragüete Riesco et al. report that regions with lower log(FF) values exhibit higher PAH-to-dust ratio R_PAH, indicating less efficient PAH processing (i.e., more PAH survival) in more porous/low-FF structures.

Vasiliev & Nath report that in bubbles evolving in a clumpy medium dust can be dispersed into the hot gas on longer timescales (exceeding several Myr) for SN explosions more frequent than one SN per 30 kyr, allowing the bubble to remain a bright IR source up to several Myr.

Vasiliev & Nath state that the forward shock of the bubble moves in the interclump low-density medium and maintains high velocity there, while parts of the shock that interact with dense clumps penetrate them with lower velocity and form hot envelopes around the clumps, which supply dust into the hot gas.

Vasiliev & Nath report that continuous SNe produce multiple shocks and high-velocity sound waves that strip surviving dense clumps and replenish dust into the hot gas, increasing the duration that dust and hot tenuous gas coexist in the bubble interior.

Vasiliev & Nath report that for bubbles driven by multiple SNe the IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratio typically ranges between ≈1–30, weakly dependent on SN rate but sensitive to the ambient medium density contrast (σ); decreasing density contrast reduces IR emission and thus the observable dust signature.

Comparison — presence and persistence: the H II regions paper emphasizes low volumetric filling factors (log(FF) down to ≈ -5) associated with diffuse ionized gas that favors PAH survival, whereas the multiple-SNe bubble paper emphasizes a persistent hot, low-density plasma (T_X ∼ 2–4×10^6 K) inside bubbles that can be long-lived (dust dispersed into hot gas for > several Myr) when SN cadence is high and the medium is clumpy.

Comparison — controlling factors and observational signatures: the H II region study attributes the amount and observational signature of low-density/volume-filling ionized gas primarily to ionizing photon rate, volumetric Hα luminosity density, and filling factor (which control PAH photodissociation and R_PAH), while the SNe bubble study attributes the amount and observables of hot tenuous gas to SN rate (cadence), ambient medium clumpiness/density contrast (σ), and shock–clump interactions (which control dust replenishment, IR vs X-ray emission and dust survival).

Method/observable differences relevant to low-density gas: Aragüete Riesco et al. use Hα-based volumetric luminosity density, ionizing photon rate, filling factor and JWST/MIRI PAH-to-dust ratio R_PAH as diagnostics of porosity and PAH survival, whereas Vasiliev & Nath use 3-D hydrodynamical simulations of clustered SNe, tracking gas temperature, shock propagation, clump stripping and dust sputtering to predict X-ray and IR emission and dust survival timescales.

results.question: Compare the two studies "Not all cores are equal: Phase-space origins of dynamical friction, stalling and buoyancy" and "From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction": based on the excerpts, how do the dynamical-friction phase-space effects identified in the first paper (plateaus and DF-inflections causing stalling or buoyancy, and the capacity of inspiraling perturbers to reshape the DF) bear on the formation and central migration/merging of massive compact objects (over-massive black holes and compact stellar systems) in the LRD formation scenario described in the second paper? Provide a concise synthesis citing supported statements from each paper.
results.reference_answer:
The two papers are complementary: the DF-phase-space effects from "Not all cores are equal" imply mechanisms that can help explain, modulate, or stall the inward migration and central coalescence invoked in the LRD formation scenario in "From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction". Specifically:

- From "Not all cores are equal": core stalling arises when the host DF develops a plateau that halts inspiral, while dynamical buoyancy can push masses outward when the DF has an inflection; moreover, an inspiraling perturber can reshape the DF, erasing plateaus or creating inflections and thereby changing whether friction continues (evidence_id: 1cae81ac2ad0f0b8249af2d9; b39c49573c4cc4625e188a56).

- From the LRD scenario: LRD formation relies on many star clusters migrating and merging into a central compact stellar system and on formation/merging of over-massive black holes; cluster migration and inward coalescence are central steps in producing the compact central object (evidence_id: 772c200ac6ac54fc84a47dfd; 65304e96ebbfc540f97342bc).

Synthesis: if real galactic hosts that produce LRDs have DFs that develop plateaus or inflections, the migration of clusters and embedded BH seeds could be slowed, stalled off-center, or even reversed by the DF-driven dynamics described in the first paper. Conversely, sufficiently massive inspiraling clusters or BHs could modify the host DF during their approach (erasing plateaus or creating negative gradients), enabling further inward migration and merger—this provides a nonlinear, feedback-regulated pathway that can lengthen or accelerate the timescale for central coalescence in the LRD channel. Thus, the phase-space criteria identified in "Not all cores are equal" are directly relevant to whether the cluster-driven formation and central assembly of over-massive BHs and compact stellar systems in the LRD scenario proceed efficiently or get stalled/wander, and predict that migration outcomes depend on the host DF structure as well as the perturber mass (evidence_id: 1cae81ac2ad0f0b8249af2d9; b39c49573c4cc4625e188a56; 772c200ac6ac54fc84a47dfd; 65304e96ebbfc540f97342bc).

Dattathri et al. ("Not all cores are equal") state that the host distribution function (DF), not just the central density gradient, determines the efficiency and direction of dynamical friction, with core stalling arising when a perturber encounters a plateau in the DF. [1]

Dattathri et al. state that dynamical buoyancy emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection (d f / d E > 0), which drives an unstable dipole mode that pushes a central mass outward. [2]

Dattathri et al. report that an inspiraling perturber can dynamically reshape the host DF—erasing existing plateaus and re-establishing negative gradients—or can create new inflections in the DF that then cause stalling. [3] [4]

Dutta Chowdhury et al. ("From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction") propose that clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and black holes to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk. [5]

The LRD paper estimates that ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters can migrate to the galaxy center mostly by two-body segregation (aided by disk dynamical friction) on a timescale of order ∼100 Myr. [6] [7]

The LRD paper reports that migrating clusters merge into compact central stellar systems with mass M ∼ 10^9 M⊙ within radii of R ∼ 60 pc. [6]

The LRD paper states that young, rotating clusters are sites for BH-seed formation: core collapse can produce a ≃10^4 M⊙ BH seed in less than 3 Myr in ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters, and observed LRD BH masses are reported in the range 10^6.7–10^8.7 M⊙ with high BH-to-stellar mass ratios. [6] [8]

The LRD paper’s provided excerpts document cluster migration mechanisms (two-body segregation and disk dynamical friction), migration timescales (~100 Myr for ~10^6 M⊙ clusters), and that migrating clusters carry BH seeds and merge at the galaxy center, but they do not report that DF plateaus, DF-inflections, dynamical-friction stalling, or dynamical buoyancy (as defined by Dattathri et al.) actually operate or are observed during cluster/BH migration in the LRD/compaction context. ## 9. CONCLUSIONS 

Dynamical friction, long treated as a robust and universal drag force, proves far more nuanced than the classic Chandrasekhar (1943) formalism, which assumes an infinite, homogeneous, and isotropic background medium. These discrepancies are especially prominent in systems with central cores, in which previous studies have shown that dynamical friction ceases to be efficient (core stalling) or even reverse in direction (dynamical buoyancy). However, it has remained unclear what the detailed criteria are under which these phenomena operate. 

Our study demonstrates that the efficacy and direction of dynamical friction depend not on the central density gradient alone but on the underlying phase-space structure encoded in the distribution function (DF). Using idealized, highresolution _𝑁_ -body simulations and analytic arguments from kinetic theory, we have shown that core stalling and dynamical buoyancy arise from distinct features in the DF: 

- **Stalling** occurs when the inspiraling perturber reaches a plateau in the DF, that is,

- **Buoyancy** emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection (d _𝑓_ /d _𝐸>_ 0), rendering them unstable to a growing dipole mode that drives the central mass outward. 

Crucially, these DF features are not uniquely tied to a specific density slope: systems with similar surface densities or

Not all cores are equal 

core sizes can behave dramatically differently depending on how sharply their outer and inner density slopes transition. In the case of double power-law ( _𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾_ ) models, systems with low _𝛾_ (shallow inner slope) and/or high _𝛼_ (sharp transition) naturally develop plateaus and inflections, explaining why apparently “similar” cores yield dissimilar dynamical outcomes. Hence, not all cores are equal. 

The DF framework also clarifies why more massive perturbers can transiently overcome the stalling barrier: their inspiral dynamically reshapes the DF, erasing existing plateaus and re-establishing negative gradients that re-enable friction. Conversely, lighter objects remain trapped at the plateau, producing long-lived off-center configurations. In addition, even if the DF initially does not have a plateau or inflection, the BH inspiral itself can create an inflection, resulting in its stalling. This self-regulated interplay between the perturber and its host distribution reveals dynamical friction as a fundamentally nonlinear, feedback-driven process, not a static background drag. 

Our results bridge the gap between kinetic theory and cosmological structure formation, offering a unified physical picture of friction, stalling, and buoyancy in cored systems. Future work will extend this framework to more realistic, anisotropic, and time-evolving galaxies, enabling quantitative predictions for the demographics of stalled and wandering black holes across cosmic time. The astrophysical implications are far-reaching. In dwarf galaxies and massive ellipticals, core stalling provides a natural explanation for displaced nuclear star clusters and off-centered AGN. It also accounts for globular clusters in dwarf galaxies which would have otherwise sunk to the center. For SMBH binaries, stalling and buoyancy identify a key bottleneck in the inspiral process prior to binary formation and gravitational-wave emission, influencing predicted merger rates for LISA. This underscores the necessity for an in-depth study of core formation via different mechanisms, focusing in particular on their phase-space distributions, and the resulting dynamics in these systems. One of these mechanisms, self-interacting dark matter, is studied in a follow-up paper (van den Bosch & Dattathri 2026).

retrieved_chunks.text: However, once the BH approaches a plateau in the DF and slows down, non-linear effects become increasingly relevant. Chief among these is orbit trapping, whereby a particle crosses the separatrix associated with the perturber and becomes trapped into libration (e.g., Henrard 1982; Tremaine & Weinberg 1984). Since the trapped particles have different libration frequencies, they phase-mix over time if the libration zone does not evolve significantly over time (which is true during stalling of low-mass perturbers). Importantly, the orbit can become untrapped when it crosses the separatrix again, either because of some chaotic behavior or because the separatrix itself evolves. Separatrix crossing, and the associated phasemixing, is a non-reversible effect, resulting in large changes in the system’s DF (Chiba & Schönrich 2022; see also Kodama et al. 2026). For example, in the `RapidCore` system, non-linear effects become relevant once the BH reaches the stalling radius, where (∇ _𝑓_ )CR ≈ 0. Now, orbit trapping works towards erasing the inflection in the DF, beyond what the dipole instability is able to do (cf. Figures 5 and 6). Nonlinear effects can also become important when the BH has sunk in to a radius where its mass becomes comparable to the enclosed mass. An example of this is the sinking of the BH in the `GradualCore` system shown in the right-hand columns of Figure 6. Here, the initial DF does not have any inflection or plateau that would give rise to stalling. However, once the BH reaches _𝑟_ BH ≃ 0 _._ 21, the enclosed mass becomes comparable to the BH mass and non-linear effects, including orbit trapping works towards _creating_ a plateau in the DF, which subsequently causes the perturber to stall. Over time, this newly created inflection is eroded over time and the BH begins to slowly sink in again once the DF has evolved sufficiently such that (∇ _𝑓_ )CR _<_ 0.

## ABSTRACT 

Dynamical friction governs the orbital decay of massive perturbers within galaxies and dark matter halos, yet its standard Chandrasekhar formulation fails in systems with cores of (roughly) constant density, where inspiral can halt or even reverse, phenomena known respectively as core stalling and dynamical buoyancy. Although these effects have been observed in simulations, the conditions under which they arise remain unclear. Using high-resolution N-body simulations and analytic insights from kinetic theory, we systematically explore the physical origin of these effects. We demonstrate that the overall distribution function (DF) of the host, not just its central density gradient, determines the efficiency and direction of dynamical friction. Core stalling arises when the perturber encounters a plateau in the DF, either pre-existing or dynamically created through its own inspiral, while buoyancy emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection that drives an unstable dipole mode. We show that double power-law density profiles with rapid outer-to-inner slope transitions naturally produce such DF features, which is why structurally similar cores can yield radically different dynamical outcomes. Our results provide a unified framework linking the phase-space structure of galaxies to the fate of embedded massive objects, with direct implications for off-center AGN, the dynamics of nuclear star clusters, and the stalled coalescence of black holes in dwarf galaxies and massive ellipticals. 

_Keywords:_ Galaxy evolution – Galaxy dynamics – Orbital resonances – N-body simulations

In addition, both the enclosed mass model and the tidal radius model predict that the stalling radius increases with perturber mass. This may be the case if the system’s DF initially has no inflection or plateau, since a more massive perturber will induce a stronger response, leading to larger changes in the DF. However, in systems that already have a plateau in the DF, such as the `RapidCore` system, perturbers stall at the same radius independent of their mass (Figure 4). 

Banik & van den Bosch (2022) formulate a non-perturbative treatment of dynamical friction by treating dynamical friction as a restricted three-body problem. By integrating orbits that are close to resonances with the perturber, they show that outside the core, the near-resonant orbits exert a net negative torque on the perturber, resulting in friction. However, inside the core, following a bifurcation in the Lagrange points, some of the near-resonant orbits exert a net positive torque, resulting in buoyancy. Hence, they argue that stalling should occur at or near this bifurcation radius, _𝑟_ bif (Banik 2023). Importantly, bifurcation strictly only occurs in perfectly harmonic cores ( _𝛾_ = 0). For the two _𝛾_ = 0 profiles considered here, for _𝑀_ BH = 10[−][3] , the _𝛼_ = 1 system has _𝑟_ bif = 0 _._ 194, and the _𝛼_ = 2 system has _𝑟_ bif = 0 _._ 368, which are slightly larger but in reasonable agreement with the _𝑁_ -body results in Figure 3. The exact role of bifurcation in stalling and buoyancy is left for future work.

The major compaction events, those that trigger a decisive long-term quenching process and a transition from central dark-matter to baryon dominance, tend to occur near the golden mass, halos of masses 10[11] −10[12] _𝑀_ ⊙ (A. Dekel et al. 2019) at all redshifts. Thisis seenin cosmological simulations (M. Tomassetti et al. 2016) and in machine-learning-aided comparisons to observations (M. Huertas-Company et al. 2018). This preferred mass scale for major compaction events seems to be due, at least partly, to the physical processes of supernova feedback and hot circum-galactic medium (CGM), which tend to suppress compaction attempts at lower and higher masses, respectively. At cosmic dawn, the FFB halos are indeed of masses ∼ 10[11] _𝑀_ ⊙, in the vicinity of the golden mass, and they correspond to high-sigma peaks of _>_ 4 _𝜎_ (A. Dekel et al. 2025a), which tend to have more frequent and stronger compaction events due to multiple colliding streams with low angular momentum (Y. Dubois et al. 2012). 

The compaction events trigger a sequence of morphological changes, which may be relevant both to the beginning and the end of the LRD phase. The compaction events drive central starbursts in the form of blue nuggets, followed by insideout quenching to quiescent red nuggets, as a result of gas depletion due to star formation and the associated outflows (S. Tacchella et al. 2016b,a). 

We use here cosmological simulations, utilizing a variety of codes and physical models at different epochs, to quantify the compaction-driven growth of compact, massive central stellar systems, beyond their growth by dry mergers between the clusters. These compact central stellar systems could plausibly be identified with the stellar systems of LRDs, and could possibly increase the escape velocities to the level that is required for retaining the SMBHs at the centers against GW recoils.

## 9. CONCLUSION 

We propose that the Little Red Dots, as detected in JWST observations, form naturally at cosmic morning, _𝑧_ = 4 − 8, as compact stellar systems with over-massive black holes. The two key elements in the proposed scenario are (a) the thousands of star clusters that form at cosmic dawn, _𝑧>_ 8, in a phase of feedback-free starbursts within the clusters, and (b) wet compaction events that are associated with mergers or colliding cold streams. Our conclusions regarding four central elements of LRD formation can be summarized as follows.

## ABSTRACT 

We address the origin of the Little Red Dots (LRDs) seen by JWST at cosmic morning ( _𝑧_ = 4−8) as compact stellar systems with over-massive black holes (BHs). We propose that LRDs form naturally after feedbackfree starbursts (FFB) in thousands of star clusters and following wet compaction. Analytically, we show how the clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and BHs to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk. The clusters merge to form compact central stellar systems as observed. Mutual tidal stripping does not qualitatively affect the analysis. The young, rotating clusters are natural sites for the formation of BH seeds via rapid core collapse. The migrating clusters carry the BH seeds, which merge into central super-massive BHs (SMBHs). Compactions are required to deepen the potential wells such that the SMBHs are retained after post-merger gravitational-wave recoils, locked to the galaxy centers. Using cosmological simulations at different epochs, with different codes and physical recipes, we evaluate the additional growth of LRD-matching compact central stellar systems by global compaction events. Adding to the dry growth by cluster mergers, the compactions can increase the escape velocities to retain the SMBHs. The LRDs appear at _𝑧_ ∼ 8, after the formation of FFB clusters, and disappear after _𝑧_ ∼ 4 when the stellar mass is above 10[9] _𝑀_ ⊙ by growing post-compaction blue disks around the nuclear LRDs. The LRD abundance is expected to be ∼ 10[−][5] −10[−][4] Mpc[−][3] , increasing from _𝑧_ ∼ 4 to _𝑧_ ∼ 8.

## 9.2. _Over-massive black holes_ 

Regarding the growth of over-massive black holes in the LRDs, we find the following: 

• A. Dekel et al. (2025b), following others, demonstrated that the FFB clusters are natural sites for the formation of BH seeds via rapid core collapse. The core collapse into a 10[4] _𝑀_ ⊙ BH seed occurs in less than 3 Myr in young, rotating clusters of ∼ 10[6] _𝑀_ ⊙. It is driven by gravo-thermal instability, which is governed by the massive stars that are still present during the first ∼ 3 Myr. The core collapse is sped by gravo-gyro instability as long as the clusters are supported by rotation induced by their host disks. 

• The migrating clusters then carry with them the BH seeds, making them ready for merging at the galaxy center into an over-massive BH. 

• Extending the analysis of A. Dekel et al. (2025b), we showed that further deepening of the central potential well is needed in order to retain the SMBH in the galaxy against post-merger GW recoils, and in order to lock it to the galaxy center. This is higher than the compactness produced by dry migration of clusters, which is expected to lead to an escape velocity of _𝑉_ esc ∼ 300 km s[−][1] .

## 3.3. _Migration summary_ 

Figure 1 summarizes the different timescales for migration from the disk half-mass radius to the center as a function of cluster mass for typical FFB galaxies. They are computed for a fiducial FFB disk of clusters (§2). Shown are the timescales for two-body segregation (eq. 8), for dynamical friction by a hot disk (eq. 22, with _𝐹_ d = 1) with a smoothed component fraction _𝑠_ = 0 _._ 1 and _𝑠_ = 0 _._ 5, and for dynamical friction by the halo (eq. 17, with _𝐹_ h = 1). Note that in the segregation timescale _𝑀_ c stands for the maximum cluster mass, while in the dynamical friction estimates it refers to a certain average cluster mass. We learn that the two-body segregation timescale dominates the migration. For _𝑀_ c ∼ 10[6] _𝑀_ ⊙ it is estimated to bring half the clusters to the center in ∼ 100 Myr. Clusters of higher maximum mass of ∼ 10[7] _𝑀_ ⊙ will get to the center in ∼ 20 Myr.The dynamical friction by the disk operates on a longer timescale in the early stages of the migration when _𝑠_ is small. If and when the stripped mass into a smooth component reaches half the disk mass, _𝑠_ ∼ 0 _._ 5 (see §5 for estimates of _𝑠_ ), the dynamical friction timescale becomes comparable to the segregation timescale. The dynamical friction by the halo is estimated to provide a less important contribution, operating on a timescale of a few Gigayears.

## 9.1. _Dry evolution of clusters_ 

Investigating the dry evolution of the galactic disk of FFB clusters using analytic toy-modeling, we learned the following: 

• The 10[6] _𝑀_ ⊙ clusters allow efficient migration to the galaxy center, mostly by two-body segregation aided by dynamical friction against the disk, on a timescale of ∼ 100 Myr (and shorter for more massive clusters). 

• The clusters merge into compact central stellar systems, containing _𝑀_ ∼ 10[9] _𝑀_ ⊙ within radii of _𝑅_ ∼ 60 pc, These are already in the ball park of the stellar systems deduced from observed LRDs using a hybrid model of stars and BHs. 

• Mutual tidal stripping leaves most of the cluster mass intact such that it does not make a qualitative difference to the analysis. The part of the mass that is stripped into a smooth component allows the disk to assist the migration by exerting dynamical friction on the clusters. 

• Simulations of dry evolution of clusters with BHs (Dutta Chowdhury et al., in preparation) and high-resolution cosmological simulations at cosmic dawn (H.-Z. Chen et al. 2026), reproduce the predicted rate of cluster migration and the formation of a massive, compact, central stellar system via cluster-cluster mergers.

claims.text: Dattathri et al. ("Not all cores are equal") state that the host distribution function (DF), not just the central density gradient, determines the efficiency and direction of dynamical friction, with core stalling arising when a perturber encounters a plateau in the DF.
Dattathri et al. state that dynamical buoyancy emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection (d f / d E > 0), which drives an unstable dipole mode that pushes a central mass outward.

Dattathri et al. report that an inspiraling perturber can dynamically reshape the host DF—erasing existing plateaus and re-establishing negative gradients—or can create new inflections in the DF that then cause stalling.

Dutta Chowdhury et al. ("From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction") propose that clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and black holes to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk.
The LRD paper estimates that ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters can migrate to the galaxy center mostly by two-body segregation (aided by disk dynamical friction) on a timescale of order ∼100 Myr.
The LRD paper reports that migrating clusters merge into compact central stellar systems with mass M ∼ 10^9 M⊙ within radii of R ∼ 60 pc.

The LRD paper states that young, rotating clusters are sites for BH-seed formation: core collapse can produce a ≃10^4 M⊙ BH seed in less than 3 Myr in ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters, and observed LRD BH masses are reported in the range 10^6.7–10^8.7 M⊙ with high BH-to-stellar mass ratios.

The LRD paper’s provided excerpts document cluster migration mechanisms (two-body segregation and disk dynamical friction), migration timescales (~100 Myr for ~10^6 M⊙ clusters), and that migrating clusters carry BH seeds and merge at the galaxy center, but they do not report that DF plateaus, DF-inflections, dynamical-friction stalling, or dynamical buoyancy (as defined by Dattathri et al.) actually operate or are observed during cluster/BH migration in the LRD/compaction context.

missing_details: No direct evidence in the provided LRD excerpts that DF plateaus, DF-inflections, stalling, or buoyancy actually operate during cluster/BH migration in the LRD scenario, or that migrating clusters/BHs in that context reshape the host DF as described for the cored systems in Dattathri et al.

a0001.text: Dattathri et al. ("Not all cores are equal") state that the host distribution function (DF), not just the central density gradient, determines the efficiency and direction of dynamical friction, with core stalling arising when a perturber encounters a plateau in the DF.

a0002.text: Dattathri et al. state that dynamical buoyancy emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection (d f / d E > 0), which drives an unstable dipole mode that pushes a central mass outward.

a0003.text: Dattathri et al. report that an inspiraling perturber can dynamically reshape the host DF—erasing existing plateaus and re-establishing negative gradients—or can create new inflections in the DF that then cause stalling.

a0004.text: Dutta Chowdhury et al. ("From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction") propose that clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and black holes to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk.

a0005.text: The LRD paper estimates that ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters can migrate to the galaxy center mostly by two-body segregation (aided by disk dynamical friction) on a timescale of order ∼100 Myr.

a0006.text: The LRD paper reports that migrating clusters merge into compact central stellar systems with mass M ∼ 10^9 M⊙ within radii of R ∼ 60 pc.

a0007.text: The LRD paper states that young, rotating clusters are sites for BH-seed formation: core collapse can produce a ≃10^4 M⊙ BH seed in less than 3 Myr in ∼10^6 M⊙ clusters, and observed LRD BH masses are reported in the range 10^6.7–10^8.7 M⊙ with high BH-to-stellar mass ratios.

a0008.text: The LRD paper’s provided excerpts document cluster migration mechanisms (two-body segregation and disk dynamical friction), migration timescales (~100 Myr for ~10^6 M⊙ clusters), and that migrating clusters carry BH seeds and merge at the galaxy center, but they do not report that DF plateaus, DF-inflections, dynamical-friction stalling, or dynamical buoyancy (as defined by Dattathri et al.) actually operate or are observed during cluster/BH migration in the LRD/compaction context.

results.question: Compare the concrete methodological validations and main empirical limitations reported in "Theoretical emission lines and metallicity calibrations of H II regions in ASTRID simulation" and "The initial conditions and initial mass functions of Alpha Persei, Pleiades and Praesepe": specifically, what validation does each study report for its modeling approach, and what primary limitation or problematic result does each paper identify that affects the reliability of its key inferences?
results.reference_answer: Validation: The ASTRID emission-line study validates its nebular emission modelling by comparing the predicted [O III] 5007 luminosity functions to recent high-redshift observational constraints, finding good agreement in slope and number density with JWST/NIRCam WFSS (Matthee et al. 2023) and FRESCO (Meyer et al. 2024) (evidence_id: adf9bb9dd76c737c68dd5984). The open-cluster IMF study validates its inference framework by combining Gaia DR3 proper motions/parallaxes (with UKIDSS and Hipparcos supplements), Bayesian photometric modelling of binaries, and a grid of N-body simulations to train an emulator; this combined approach yields membership probabilities and constrained initial conditions (evidence_id: 823aab803438c34ad6535e3b). Primary limitation/problematic result: The ASTRID paper identifies a non-physical insensitivity of the N2O2 UV metallicity diagnostic tied to a problematic N/O abundance ratio in the simulation, and it also underpredicts high-excitation R3 in low-mass galaxies at z>6 indicating missing physics (evidence_id: 7d193908ee0445d43fa573af; 39ecfac5a7e1ba72724cccad). The open-cluster study highlights systematic uncertainties from mass–luminosity conversions at low masses (affecting the measured low-mass IMF slope) and possible survivor bias or environmental/dependence ambiguities at high mass, limiting confidence in claims about IMF universality (evidence_id: 2b97e92a96faae53e9459f8c; 117f4ed4c4b340415aa5c08b).
results.answer:
The ASTRID paper validates its nebular-emission modeling by reproducing empirical SFR indicators: it reports model-derived conversion factors C_Hα ≃ 41.357 and C_[O II] ≃ 41.015 that are in excellent agreement with established literature calibrations, and by producing [O iii] λ5007 luminosity functions across z = 2–7 that are broadly consistent with recent JWST observations. [1] [2]

The ASTRID paper identifies a primary problematic result limiting reliability: its models predict the N2O2 UV diagnostic to be largely insensitive to metallicity with large scatter and strong redshift dependence, a behaviour it attributes to a problematic N/O abundance ratio in the ASTRID simulation and therefore cautions that the N2O2 UV relation should not be used until nitrogen enrichment is better understood. [3] [4]

The open-cluster paper validates its inference of initial conditions and IMFs by verifying best-fitting parameters with N-body simulations: it ran at least 20 simulations per cluster and found the simulations reproduce the observed number of stars, binary fraction, half-mass radius and three mass-function slopes within 2.5σ (with most parameters agreeing within 1σ). [5] [6]

The open-cluster paper identifies a primary limitation from its modelling assumptions: it assumes gas-free initial conditions, whereas inclusion of instantaneous gas expulsion (per Weis et al. 2025) can remove up to ≈75% of the initial cluster mass and, in that study, leads to a very different inferred IMF for Praesepe (high-mass slope α_h = 4.1 and low-mass slope α_l = 0.4), indicating sensitivity of inferred initial IMFs to the gas-expulsion assumption. [7]

## _5.6.2 Evaluation of calibration performance_ 

We quantified the uncertainty of the derived metallicities using the 68% confidence interval of the posterior distribution, defined as ( _𝜎_ 84 − _𝜎_ 16)/2. The results for single-variable and two-variable diagnostics as a function of line ratio and S/N are presented in Fig. 10 and Fig. 11, respectively. In these figures, solid, dashed, and dotted lines correspond to H _𝛽_ relative errors of 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1. For reference, in the JWST JADES DR4 NIRSpec R1000_5pix catalog, 0.2%, 7%, and 24% of targets at _𝑧_ = 5 − 7 can meet the above high, moderate and low S/N requirements, respectively. 

Our analysis yields several key insights regarding the stability and precision of different calibrations: 

(i) Common Diagnostics (R23, R3, and R2): The R23 diagnostic emerges as the most robust calibration overall. It is remarkably insensitive to S/N variations, maintaining a dispersion of ( _𝜎_ 84 − _𝜎_ 16)/2 ≃ 0 _._ 1 dex over most of its dynamic range. However, a significant limitation arises in the “turnover” region (log R23 ≃ 0.8), where the upper and lower metallicity branches merge. In this regime, the degeneracy leads to broad PDFs, causing uncertainties to spike to ∼ 0 _._ 3 dex. The R2 and R3 calibrations exhibit similar behavior due to their inherent double-branched nature.
